blocks.text: Dynamic prompt generation assembles a prompt structure at runtime based on the current situation, available tools, retrieved memory, trajectory state, rather than filling fixed slots in an otherwise unchanging template, covered in the earlier Template-Based Prompting topic.

This topic covers how dynamic generation differs from a fixed template, assembling prompts from variable components at runtime, including or excluding sections based on current state, the real risk of unpredictability this flexibility introduces, and when a fixed template genuinely remains the better choice.
1. What Dynamic Prompt Generation Means

blocks.alt: Building on multi-agent communication, dynamic prompt generation assembles the prompt at runtime

blocks.text: Dynamic prompt generation constructs the actual structure of a prompt at the moment it is needed, based on the specific situation an agent currently finds itself in, rather than always following the same fixed layout with only the variable content changing.
2. Dynamic Generation vs Fixed Templates

blocks.alt: A fixed template keeps the same structure with filled slots, dynamic generation changes the structure itself

blocks.text: The earlier Template-Based Prompting topic covered a template with a fixed structure and variable slots that get filled with different data, dynamic prompt generation goes further, the actual sections and structure present in the prompt can differ from one call to the next, based on what is genuinely relevant at that moment.

blocks.text: 3. Assembling a Prompt From Variable Components

blocks.alt: Available tools, retrieved memory, and current trajectory state combine into an assembled prompt

blocks.text: A dynamically generated prompt is built by combining whichever components are actually relevant right now, the tools currently available, any memory retrieved for this specific situation, the accumulated trajectory so far, assembled fresh for this specific moment rather than pulled from one fixed layout.
4. Including or Excluding Sections Based on State

blocks.alt: A relevant section gets included, an irrelevant section gets excluded

blocks.text: A section genuinely relevant to the current step, retrieved memory when memory actually applies, gets included, a section not relevant, that same memory section when nothing relevant was retrieved, gets excluded entirely, this connects directly to the context window optimization concerns covered in an earlier module, only including what is genuinely needed.
5. Using a Model to Help Construct the Next Prompt

blocks.alt: A model call helps construct the next prompt, a meta level of prompt generation

blocks.text: In more advanced setups, a model call itself can help decide what the next prompt should actually contain, effectively a meta level of prompting, one call reasoning about what information the next call genuinely needs, before that next call is actually assembled and sent.

blocks.title: This adds real complexity worth using deliberately
blocks.content: A meta level prompt generation step is a genuinely more complex, harder to debug pattern than either a fixed template or a straightforward rule based assembly, reserve it for situations where the added flexibility clearly earns its complexity.

blocks.text: 6. The Risk of Unpredictability

blocks.alt: Poorly controlled assembly leads to inconsistent behavior

blocks.text: The same flexibility that makes dynamic generation powerful also makes it riskier, a poorly controlled assembly process can produce meaningfully different prompt structures for what should be very similar situations, producing inconsistent behavior that is genuinely harder to predict and debug than a fixed template would be.
7. Testing Dynamically Generated Prompts

This connects directly to the prompt debugging and iteration practices covered in an earlier module, testing a dynamic prompt generation system needs to cover a genuinely representative range of the different situations it could actually encounter, not just one or two example states, since the assembled structure itself varies across those situations.
8. A Worked Example of Dynamic Assembly

An agent working through a multi-step research task assembles a different prompt structure at each step, early steps include a full goal description and available tool list, later steps, once the goal has been clarified through earlier reasoning, include a condensed goal summary and only the specific tools relevant to the current remaining work.
9. When Fixed Templates Are Still the Better Choice

blocks.alt: A simple, stable task fits a fixed template better, a highly variable task fits dynamic generation better

blocks.text: For a task with a genuinely consistent shape across every call, a fixed template, covered in an earlier module, remains simpler, more predictable, and easier to test and debug, dynamic generation earns its added complexity specifically for tasks where the relevant prompt content genuinely varies enough that a single fixed structure would not serve every situation well.
Worked Example

A team building a multi-purpose agent initially uses one large fixed template including every possible section, tool descriptions, full memory context, and complete trajectory history, regardless of whether all of it is actually relevant to the current step, leading to bloated prompts and occasional confusion when irrelevant sections distract from what actually matters right now.

Switching to dynamic assembly that includes only the sections genuinely relevant to the current situation, tools only when a tool call is actually being considered, memory only when something relevant was retrieved, produces more focused, more effective prompts, while requiring more careful testing across the genuinely varied situations the agent now encounters.
Common Mistakes

items: Using dynamic prompt generation for a task simple and consistent enough that a fixed template would have worked just as well
Assembling a prompt so unpredictably that similar situations produce meaningfully different, inconsistent structures
Not testing dynamically generated prompts across a genuinely representative range of the situations they will actually encounter
Adding meta level prompt generation complexity without a clear need that justifies the added difficulty of debugging it

blocks.text: Practice

Take an agent task where prompt content genuinely varies across steps, sketch out which sections should be included or excluded at two different, meaningfully different points in the trajectory, and consider what testing would be needed to confirm the assembly logic behaves consistently across both.
Key Takeaway

Dynamic prompt generation assembles the actual structure of a prompt at runtime based on the current situation, rather than filling fixed slots in an unchanging template, offering real flexibility for genuinely variable tasks at the cost of added unpredictability and testing burden, making it worth reserving for cases where a fixed template genuinely could not serve every situation well.
